questions.q: In the Meridian Fixtures case study, why is the company's three-org structure identified as a problem worth examining?
options: Because having more than one Salesforce org is always wrong under any circumstances
Because Salesforce technically limits every company to a single org
Because the three orgs were all built by the same contractor

Because it accumulated through acquisitions with no documented Reference Architecture ever defining when an additional org is actually warranted -- an accidental rather than deliberate multi-org strategy
questions.explain: The case study frames Meridian's three-org structure as accidental: each org exists because of how an acquisition happened, not because of a documented, deliberate Reference Architecture decision, which is the distinction Lesson 12 draws between justified and accidental multi-org.

questions.q: What does this lesson suggest is the most likely actual root cause of the data warehouse's reconciliation failures at Meridian?
options: A bug purely inside the data warehouse's own reporting logic, unrelated to anything upstream
The data warehouse not having enough storage capacity
Three inconsistent ERP integration patterns, built by different contractors at different times, feeding structurally different orgs into one warehouse that assumes a single consistent shape
Meridian's customers submitting incorrect data directly into the warehouse
questions.explain: The lesson argues the warehouse's reconciliation failures are a symptom, not the root cause -- the actual root cause is the inconsistent integration patterns across three orgs feeding data at different cadences and shapes into a warehouse expecting consistency.

questions.q: Why does the case study say an undecided system-of-record question for shared customer data is itself diagnostic?
options: Because it proves Meridian has no customers who interact with multiple business units
Because it means the ERP is definitely the system of record for everything by default
Because undecided questions never cause any real business impact
Because an undecided system-of-record question is exactly the kind of gap that produces the silent data drift Lesson 3 describes
questions.explain: The lesson connects Meridian's undecided system-of-record question directly to Lesson 3's dueling-systems-of-record concept -- not having a decision at all is itself a sign of the exact gap that causes drift.

questions.q: In the sequenced recommendation this lesson proposes for Meridian, what should be addressed first, and why?
options: The data warehouse's reports, since fixing the symptom first buys time for everything else
Establishing a governance body with real decision rights, since nothing else (multi-org strategy, system-of-record assignment, integration standardization) holds without it
Hiring a fourth contractor to build a fourth, newer integration pattern
Immediately merging all three orgs into one without any further analysis
questions.explain: The lesson's proposed sequence starts with establishing governance, reasoning that none of the other decisions (multi-org strategy, system-of-record assignment, integration standardization) can be made and held centrally without a governance body with real authority.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what does the case study recommend happens to the data warehouse reconciliation problem once the upstream integration inconsistency is fixed?
options: It will definitely get worse
It is likely to resolve substantially, rather than needing an independent warehouse-side fix, since the inconsistency feeding it was the actual root cause
It is completely unrelated and will not change at all
It will require Meridian to delete the data warehouse entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's recommendation places warehouse reconciliation last specifically because it's expected to improve substantially once the upstream integration-pattern inconsistency driving it is addressed, rather than needing to be patched independently.
